newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS - Australian Commodities Roundup - Oct 22.
newsitem.headline: RTRS - Australian Commodities Roundup - Oct 22.

text.p: Benchmark Chicago wheat prices opened the week hovering around $4.0 per bushel as the U.S. market eased again following a sharp drop in European grain prices. Declines follow bumper harvests after a run-up in prices earlier this year that saw Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) nearby wheat futures hit a record $7.50. A Chicago price at $4 per bushel, not seen since June 1995, equates to $159 per tonne paid by wheat importers, compared with $300 in April of this year.

Elsewhere in commodity markets crude oil prices stayed firm on strong pre-winter demand for heating fuel in the northern hemisphere at around $24.50 for a barrel of the benchmark North Sea Brent Blend.
In Chicago, the Commodities Research Bureau index rose 0.48 points to 243.83.

Copper got a modest burst of strength on Monday afternoon, regaining a foothold above $1,950 and propping up other metal prices. Three month prices finished the afternoon kerb just above the much-watched $1,950 level, but failed to re-challenge the morning high of $1,965. Last business was at $1,951, up $11. The market was wary about Tuesday's LME inventory data after a surprise fall of 19,125 tonnes of copper on Friday. Some floor traders said there was talk of a 10,000-15,000-tonne fall in stocks but others said those figures sounded a bit high.
The upturn in copper helped lift most of the other metals into positive territory, except aluminium, which lost more ground.

Aluminium scored a second session of losses after several days last week of steaming to a high of $1,376. Monday saw a steady erosion of values but they ended off their low of $1,346 at $1,352, down $7.50.
Lead popped higher after retesting Friday's 8-1/2 month low of $715 during the morning. Last kerb business was $725, up $6. Resistance was seen at $734.
Nickel closed the day marginally higher but well within recent ranges and below the $7,110 barrier. It finished at $7,070, up $15.
Tin ended barely changed at $5,980, up $5, and zinc closed firmer, probing resistance, at $1,024, also up $5.
Alloy was last quoted at $1,225/30, down from $1,230/35.

CBOT wheat futures closed lower and new contract lows were set with strong competition for exports leading the way down, traders said. Traders said the price of U.S. wheat remains steep relative to other countries which continues to cut into potential export sales of U.S. supplies. "U.S. wheat is too high priced relative to the EU and especially Argentina," said Skip Searcy, wheat trading specialist for Chicago-based grain house FIMAT Futures. Wheat closed three to 4-3/4 cents per bushel lower, with December down 4-1/4 at $4.00-1/2.

NYMEX crude broke key psychological resistance of $26.00 a barrel in Monday afternoon trade, hitting $26.05, crude's highest price since January of 1991. At 1433 EDT, November crude stood 24 cents higher at $26.03 a barrel. The rally extended gains made last week when the price of crude set new post-Gulf War highs. "There is great bullish trend here," said Jack McIntyre, market strategist with MCM Trade Watch. The oil complex spent most of Monday consolidating following last week's price gains.

CSCE world sugar futures closed weaker after a thinly-traded session in which most of the day's activity took place on the open, dealers said. Prices fell to 10.52, a nearly five-month low, pressured by follow-through fund selling. The March contract traded at 10.47 on May 31.

New York precious metals futures ended solidly higher Monday, with fund shortcovering seen leading the way, despite a bearish fundamental outlook for the complex, analysts said. "The market remains bearish, but is clearly uncomfortable everytime spot gold dips below $380 and there's been no selling pressure really in the past few days, leaving the funds a little nervous and encouraging some shortcovering," Credit Suisse New York vice president Ian MacDonald said. In New York bullion trade, spot gold ended quoted $381.75/382.25 an ounce, against the London afternoon fix at $381.00 and the New York close Friday at $380.10-380.50.
